identity.title: Blink of an eye: a simple theory for feature localization in generative models

problem.claim: The paper asks why generative models can undergo abrupt behavioral or feature changes during generation, including critical windows in diffusion models.

gap.claim: Existing critical-window theory for diffusion models relies heavily on strong distributional assumptions and Gaussian-diffusion specifics.

contributions.claim: Develops a unifying theory based on stochastic localization, attributing abrupt localization to generation concentrating on a sub-population of the modeled distribution.
Reports a framework applying to both autoregressive and diffusion models with few distributional assumptions, basic mathematical tools, and quantitatively improved diffusion-specialized bounds.
Tests the theory’s predictions on LLMs and reports that critical windows often coincide with problem-solving failures on various mathematics and reasoning benchmarks.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their theory from prior work by its cross-paradigm scope, weaker distributional assumptions, improved specialized bounds, and simpler mathematical requirements.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report quantitative improvement over previous bounds when their theory is specialized to diffusion models.
The authors report empirical validation on LLMs, where critical windows often coincide with failures across various math and reasoning benchmarks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Abrupt behavioral shifts are described in language models, while diffusion models show narrow generation windows deciding key output features.
The work introduces a unifying stochastic-localization account: generation generically localizes to a modeled-distribution sub-population.
The theory is presented as broader and less assumption-heavy than existing diffusion-focused analyses, with improved bounds and elementary mathematical requirements.
LLM experiments are reported to align critical windows with failures on multiple math and reasoning benchmarks.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links one theoretical mechanism to both autoregressive and diffusion models, then connects its predicted critical windows to LLM problem-solving failures.

lessons.interpretation: A cross-model mechanism paired with a concrete behavioral consequence can make an abstract theory easier to assess and transfer.
lessons.application: When presenting a generative-model theory, state its shared mechanism, model classes, assumption burden, and one observable prediction before reporting validation.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the proposed mechanism has not been defined across the claimed model classes or when no observable prediction is available.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the quantitative bounds, distributional assumptions, benchmark identities, failure metrics, or experimental protocols.
The reported coincidence between critical windows and failures does not establish that the windows cause the failures.
